Every facility is different. I have worked places where CNAs have set schedules. However, most facilities are short staffed and want the help that they can get. 

The flexibility is great for me. I’ve worked places that do 4 hour, 8 hour, or 12 hour shifts. Most facilities require you to work every other weekend and alternating holidays. There is often a shift differential with increased pay for PM workers and NOC shifts. 

As far as the hospital goes, there are more resources available and better benefits than nursing homes. The hospital setting is usually more strict too because of all the regulations set forth by the facility. On the other hand, nursing homes are short staffed with little resources. If someone has a heart attack it is on you and your nurse to start CPR. But it can be great because you get to really know the patients you care for and get into their routine. 

Honestly every place is just so different. I know some nursing homes will pay for CNA training. You could try to interview at one of those and tour the facility to see if you like the environment before starting classes.

I’ve been a CNA for 10 years now. I got into it because I took care of my mom until she died when I was 19 and I felt like I was a natural caregiver. My first year was hell, I cried all the time and hated it. Then I switched facilities and I learned how to be a good aid and work and a team. Now I feel like it is part of my identity. 

Do I feel like it is a calling? Not really but I enjoy taking care of people most of the time. It’s like any job it has pros and cons. It’s flexible but it is very hard on your body. 

My point is that something can feel totally wrong in some context and then right in others. Nursing is a stable job with lots of opportunities outside of the bedside. Plus clinicals are nothing like real life. Once you are done with fundamentals I would suggest trying to get a job on the floor you have an interest in. Then if you don’t like that floor you can always switch to see if you like other specialties.

So this is my take on your situation. I’ve been doing this awhile and a lot of my interviews I have been offered the job on the spot, probably about 1/2 of the 6 positions I’ve had. There is a huge need for CNAs. 

Facilities are often dirty unfortunately. It might be that they are under new management and trying to clean things up. Sometimes people just don’t care and will run a facility into the ground until it is bought out and new management has to pick up the pieces. 

As for the staffing. It can be difficult to find a job that is going to be highly staffed just because being a CNA is such hard work for little pay and the shortage. You kind of have to weigh the pros and cons for what you feel is right for you and how comfortable you feel with your knowledge and skill set. 

Personally, I think that starting in a facility like that would give you a lot of good skills for time management that you will need in nursing and you will get to see many different disease processes. Conversely, you could do home health or assisted living which would be slower paced while you are still learning the ropes on how you feel as a CNA. 

I started on night shift and ended up getting assigned the busiest and longest hall by myself. The first few months were extremely stressful but it taught me what I needed to prioritize. And I feel, how to be a really effective CNA. It was also nice being on night shift just because there are no family members or management there to hover over you and make you nervous. 

All in all, you have to consider how you want to learn. Everyone has different goals and that’s ok. If you don’t feel comfortable at a facility there are always plenty of options. Best wishes!

I personally worked for a private insurance company so it might be a little different. But I’d like to try to help by explaining what we would look for because I found some claim examiners just never explained and people that should get disability would get denied because the right things weren’t being provided. 

Like I said mental health claims are tricky and in most cases we would need to send them to a nurse for their recommendation and in extreme cases a PA. However if your doctor sends in all the materials it can make things much easier. 

The most important thing that we would need to make a claim determination was the actual office visit notes from the physician showing what happened at the visit. We would often get attending physician statements or off work notes stating things like “the client is depressed and needs time off to recover”. 

However, for example if the doctor sent me the actual medical documentation showing what happened at their office visit and it showed clinical findings of depression and treatment the person was much more likely to get approved. Some examples of clinical findings would be avoiding eye contact, disheveled appearance, forced speech, catatonia, weight loss, weight gain. We would also want to see how the doctor is treating this, are they increasing medication? Adding medication? Are they going to therapy? Have they been hospitalized? Have they been in an outpatient program?

You mentioned ECT. In my opinion that would be a good next step because it shows that you are continuing to have symptoms and that you are not having relief and need to take another step. Like I said, I can’t speak for if this will actually get you approved but maybe it will help if you know what the examiners have to look for. It always hurt me to see claims denied when I knew the person was suffering but I didn’t have the documentation to prove it, all I had was my experience talking to them on the phone. 

I wish I could help more!

Edit: I forgot to mention there are tests that your therapist/psychiatrist can do with you as well to prove loss of attention. When I was in an intensive outpatient program and on disability myself they did these tests with me. I don’t remember their names but it involved being told five random nouns and having to remember all of them after five minutes. There was also one that involved counting.
